purpose: Documents full-text editorial review of newly downloaded posts before canonical ingestion.

posts.title: Pins, Gates, and Why Jesus Was Not a Capitalist
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains why Jesus' work as a rural Galilean carpenter belonged to a subsistence economy fundamentally unlike modern capitalism.
posts.searchSummary: Explains why applying modern capitalist categories to Jesus ignores the technological and economic conditions of rural Galilee. Reconstructs how a Nazareth carpenter likely harvested and shaped wood for occasional local needs while also participating in subsistence farming and barter. Contrasts that small-scale labor with Adam Smith's specialized production, large markets, and transportation networks to show why a capitalist enterprise was impossible in Jesus' world.

posts.title: The Perpetual Virginity of Mary (and related topics)
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Distinguishes Catholic teachings about Mary's conception and virginity, then explains why the New Testament presents Jesus' brothers as biological siblings.
posts.searchSummary: Distinguishes the Immaculate Conception, virginal conception, virgin birth, and Mary's perpetual virginity as separate Catholic teachings. Examines how Jesus' named brothers and sisters in Mark and Paul conflict with perpetual virginity and surveys explanations that made them Joseph's earlier children or Jesus' cousins. Concludes that the Greek terminology and earliest traditions most naturally identify them as Mary's other biological children.

posts.title: Jesus the Carpenter?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Examines Mark's identification of Jesus as a lower-class craftsman and suggests Matthew transferred the occupation to Joseph for apologetic reasons.
posts.searchSummary: Examines Mark 6:3, the only New Testament passage identifying Jesus as a tektōn, a lower-status maker who could work in wood, stone, or metal. Compares Matthew's revision, which calls Jesus the carpenter's son, with Mark's wording and the silence of Luke and John. Suggests Matthew may have reassigned the occupation to Joseph to protect Jesus from elite contempt while creating tension with the virgin-birth narrative.

posts.title: October 2026 Gold Q&A Announcement
posts.author: jennao
posts.description: Announces the October 12 Gold and Platinum member Q&A and provides instructions for submitting questions and joining the live Zoom session.
posts.searchSummary: Announces the October 12, 2026 Gold and Platinum member Q&A scheduled for 7:00 p.m. Eastern. Explains that Bart will answer presubmitted questions during the first half before taking additional questions live from participants. Provides the online meeting information, submission instructions, and assurance that a recording will be distributed afterward to members unable to attend.

posts.title: God’s Actual Name and Another Account of the Flood
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains the origins of Yahweh and Jehovah as divine names and compares Genesis's flood narrative with the older Epic of Gilgamesh.
posts.searchSummary: Explains how the Hebrew divine name YHWH was probably pronounced Yahweh, avoided in public reading, and eventually combined with Adonai's vowels to produce Jehovah. Then compares Genesis's flood story with the older Epic of Gilgamesh, tracing shared details such as a divinely commanded boat, preserved life, a mountain landing, released birds, and sacrifice. Concludes that the Mesopotamian tradition predates and therefore could not have borrowed from Genesis.

posts.title: Interesting Questions on the Teachings of the NT
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Answers questions about a Trinitarian interpolation, Jesus' exaltation, differences between Paul and Jesus, and nonliteral truth in Christian belief.
posts.searchSummary: Answers four questions concerning New Testament teaching and Christian belief. Explains why the added Trinitarian wording in 1 John did not create the doctrine, how resurrection belief led followers to view Jesus as divine, and why Paul's atoning theology differs from Jesus' call for repentance and forgiveness. Concludes by showing how Christians can find religious truth and guidance in biblical narratives without treating every doctrine or event as literally historical.

posts.title: Modern Appearances of Jesus
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Examines modern reports of individual and group appearances of Jesus to probe how extraordinary visions and eyewitness memories should be evaluated.
posts.searchSummary: Examines documented modern claims that Jesus appeared to individuals and groups while they were awake, including cases collected by philosopher Phillip H. Wiebe. Recounts Kenneth Logie's Oakland church reports involving dozens or hundreds of witnesses, an allegedly filmed apparition, and unexplained images on the walls. Notes that the decades separating the events from Wiebe's investigation resemble the interval between Jesus' life and the earliest Gospels, raising questions about memory and evidence.
